 33 Million More Americans May Buy Crypto. For SSI Recipients, Those Coins Can Count Against a $2,000 Limit
 Millions of Americans plan to buy crypto next year, but for one group of vulnerable recipients, a single gift of Bitcoin from a relative could quietly erase their monthly benefits before they realize anything went wrong.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 1, 2026, 7:39pm ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Social Security explicitly counts digital currencies as resources, meaning SSI recipients' crypto holdings apply toward the $2,000 individual resource limit.
 Receiving crypto as a gift counts as unearned income immediately, and coins still held the next month can push recipients over the $2,000 limit, costing them eligibility.
 Bitcoin's price swings alone can flip SSI eligibility, and recipients must report value changes within 10 days or face penalties ranging from $25 to $100 per late report.

 More than 33 million U.S. adults who don’t hold crypto today are likely to buy in 2026, according to The National Cryptocurrency Association and The Harris Poll in their 2026 Crypto Readiness Report, published in early October. The findings reflect what investors plan to do. For Americans receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI), the program for older people and those with disabilities who have limited financial resources, buying crypto comes with a catch.
 Picture one of them. She’s an SSI recipient who moves part of her savings into Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) through an app. Her reasoning makes sense on the surface. Coins in a phone wallet feel separate from a checking account that shows up on a bank statement, so she assumes they won’t come up when Social Security reviews her finances.
 That assumption is where the trouble starts. Social Security’s own list of countable resources includes “digital currencies and money held in digital wallets.” 
 A $2,000 Ceiling That Hasn’t Moved in 2027
 In 2026, SSI caps countable resources at $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple. The 2027 fact sheet leaves both limits where they are, at $2,000 and $3,000.
 The test works like a snapshot. If her countable resources are over the limit at the beginning of a month, she cannot receive SSI for that month. Any crypto she can access and turn into cash counts at its value, subject to who legally owns it and the usual exceptions. Her home, one vehicle, and household goods are excluded. A Bitcoin wallet doesn’t appear anywhere on that list.
 Trading Cash for Coins Versus Receiving New Coins
 What determines the outcome is where the coins came from.
 Say she moves $500 out of a bank account that already counts toward her limit and buys Bitcoin with it. Her total doesn’t automatically go up, because one countable asset simply replaced another. The money changed form, and that’s all.
 Now say she already has $1,800 in countable resources when a relative sends her $500 in Bitcoin. Unlike buying crypto with savings she already owns, receiving it as a gift generally counts as unearned income in the month it arrives, although certain exclusions may apply. If she still holds it when the next month begins, the coins become a resource. With $2,300 in countable assets, she would exceed SSI’s $2,000 limit and could lose eligibility for that month. Crypto received as payment for work follows different income rules.
 Price Swings Can Flip Eligibility on Their Own
 Unlike cash in a bank account, Bitcoin’s value can change sharply. For someone already close to SSI’s $2,000 resource limit, even a modest price jump could push them over. The recipient wouldn’t have to buy another coin or receive another gift for that to happen.
 SSI recipients have to report new resources, sales or transfers, and changes in a resource’s value. The deadline is no later than 10 days after the end of the month in which the change happened. Each late report can bring a penalty of $25 to $100, plus any overpayment she may have to pay back. Holding the coins on an exchange or in a self-custody wallet doesn’t take them out of the resource test.
 Retirement Benefits Follow Different Rules
 Only SSI uses this asset test. Regular Social Security retirement benefits are earned through payroll taxes and have no resource limit at all. Someone collecting the average retired-worker benefit, estimated at $2,170 a month after the 2027 adjustment, can hold any amount of crypto without it affecting that check. People who get a small retirement benefit topped up by SSI still face the asset test, because the SSI part depends on it.
 What to Weigh Before Buying a First Coin
 Count crypto as cash. Treat every coin as part of the same $2,000 total as her checking account, and leave a margin below the limit so a price jump doesn’t push her over.
 Plan ahead for crypto gifts.  Receiving coins from someone else can affect SSI in the month they’re received, even if they’re spent immediately. Any coins still held the following month can also count toward the resource limit. Report gifts promptly, and don’t give away assets simply to qualify for benefits. That can create another problem under SSI’s transfer rules.
 Look into an ABLE account if eligible. People whose disability or blindness began before age 46 may qualify for these special savings accounts. Up to $100,000 can be excluded from SSI’s resource limit, giving eligible recipients more room to save.
 Crypto can be a valid choice for SSI recipients. It just counts against the same $2,000 limit as cash. A spouse’s assets, a state supplement, or how an account is titled can change the answer, so a short call to Social Security before a big move is worth making.
